## Muzzle Flash Graph

### Description

This graph shows how to combine custom mesh deformation and volume tools to create an animated muzzle-flash.

The graph produces a star-pattern muzzle-flash: a larger, central flash in the middle, with four smaller flashes pointing out and away from it.

We use visual programming to construct (from scratch) the jaggedy mesh geometry for each of the five flashes.  This is done by creating squished spheres and applying a custom (animated) noise deformer on the vertices.  Each flash mesh is then positioned, oriented, and scaled to form the star-pattern.  

The flash-meshes are merged into a single mesh, oriented to point in the desired direction, scaled, and turned into a "hot" volume with a high temperature.

A volume material with blackbody radiation is applied, causing the high-temperature voxels to glow.  Finally, to complete the "look" of the effect, a random value is used to toggle the muzzle-flash on and off, to simulate the flickering of fully automatic weapons (e.g. the muzzle-flash flickers out on random frames).

### Inputs, Controls & Outputs

The main control for this graph is simply a planar mesh that controls both the direction of the muzzle-flash, using the plane normal of the mesh, and the overall size of the effect, based on the size of the plane geometry.  

**It's important that the mesh really is a plane, because if not, there's no single 'plane normal' to use for direction.**

By default, the graph creates a unit plane mesh at the origin of the scene, oriented at a 45 degree angle.  

The intent of this graph is for users to remove the part that creates and orients the default plane and instead just drag and drop a plane from your scene into the graph.  Then, just translate the plane to where you want the muzzle-flash to happen, scale your plane up or down to make the flash big or small, and orient the plane to change the direction of the flash.

The voxel resolution and temperature of the flash can be controlled via the corresponding ports on the `make_hot_volume` compound.

There is a `chance_of_flicker` value node that controls the probability that the muzzle-flash will be not-visible on that frame.  Values close to 0 will stop any flickering, and values close to 1 will make the muzzle flash almost never visible.

### Best Practices and Tips

- To make the graph run faster you can of course make the detail size larger on the `make_hot_volume` compound, or simply output the mesh instead of the volume.  Outputting the mesh is recommended while doing layout of the muzzle-flash as it's faster than visualizing the volume.
- If for some reason you don't see a muzzle-flash by default, hit play to ensure you're not accidentally on a frame when the flash has flickered out

### Example Scene

The example scene for this graph shows how to handle multiple muzzle-flashes.

_notes.text:
By default, we construct a unit plane mesh at the origin, oriented at 45 degrees, and ensure it has point_normals since we use that to determine the

direction of the muzzle-flash.


To use a plane from your scene, you can remove this part of the graph and replace it by dragging and dropping your plane mesh and connecting it to the

"pass" node.

Note that we don't do five separate compounds for creating each of the five flash meshes. 

 Rather, the position, orientation and scale for each flash is fed to a single "create_flash_mesh" 
 compound as arrays, where each array element corresponds to one of the flash meshes.  This 
 causes the compound to automatically iterate on the input arrays, producing an array of output 
 meshes - one for each flash.

Note that the input connection to
 merge_geometry is an ARRAY - not
 a single object (hence the "hat-like" 
 appearance of the input port).  It is 
 the array of  flash meshes that were
 generated by the previous compound.

 This node, then, merges all the separate
 flash-meshes into a single mesh.
Build the relative offsets for each of the five flash meshes
